label: defpseudocomplementedlattices
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defpseudocomplementedlattices}
An algebra $\mathbf{A}=\langle A; \land,\lor,^*,0,1\rangle$ is a \emph{pseudocomplemented lattice} if the following conditions hold:

\begin{enumerate}[PS1)]
    \item $\langle A; \land,\lor,0,1\rangle$ is a bounded lattice,
    \item $x\land(x\land y)^*=x\land y^*$,
    \item $0^*=1$ and $1^*=0$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: \bf Proposition
body_md: If $\mathbf A=\langle A; \land,\lor,^*,0,1\rangle$ is a pseudocomplemented lattice, then for every $x, y \in A$, if $x\land y=0$, then $x\leq y^*$. It also holds that  $(x\lor y)^*=x^*\land y^*$.
head: environment

label: dense_element
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{dense_element}
Let $\mathbf{A}=\langle A; \land,\lor,^*,0,1\rangle$ be a pseudocomplemented lattice. We say that an element $a\in A$ is \emph{dense} if $a^*=0$. We denote by $\mathcal{D}_s(A)$ the set of all dense elements of $A$.
head: environment

label: caractdensos
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{caractdensos}
If $\mathbf H\in\mbox{$\cal SH$}$, then $x\in\mathcal{D}_s(H)$ if and only if $x=y\lor y^*$ for some $y\in H$.

label: isosemiHeytingsemiNelson
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{isosemiHeytingsemiNelson} {\rm (\cite[Theorem 5.3 and Corollary 5.2]{cornejo16semiNelson})}
If $\mathbf{A}\in\mbox{$\cal SH$}$, then $\mathbf{A}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf{sH}(\mathbf{V_k}(\mathbf A))$ through the isomorphism $g(a)=[\![(a,a^*)]\!]$. Also, if $\mathbf{A}\in\mbox{$\cal SN$}$, then $\mathbf{A}$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of $\mathbf{V_k(sH(\mathbf A))}$ through the application $h(a)=([\![a]\!],[\![\sim a]\!])$.
head: environment

label: defifiltro
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defifiltro}
Let $\mathbf{H}\in\mbox{$\cal SH$}$. A subset $F\subseteq H$ is an $i$-filter, if the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate} [\text{I}F1)]
    \item $F$ is a lattice filter of $\mathbf H$.
    \item $\mathcal{D}_s(H)\subseteq F$.
                      
    \item If $z\lor t\in F$, then for all $x\in H$, $(x\Rightarrow z)\lor(x\land t)\in F$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: ejemplofiltronoifiltro
title: \bf Example
head: environment

label: buenadefdeimplicavakarelov
title: \bf Observation
body_md:
\label{buenadefdeimplicavakarelov}
If we consider the structure $\mathbf{ N(H,F)}$, with $\mathbf{H}\in\mbox{$\cal SH$}$, an $i$-filter $F$, 
and $(a,b),(c,d)\in N(H,F)$, then (1) $c\land d=0$ and (2) $c\lor d\in F$. Notice that
$$(a\Rightarrow c)\land(a\land d)=a\land(a\Rightarrow c)\land d\underset{(SH\ref{infimoeimplicaSH})}{=}(a\land c)\land d=a\land(c\land d)\underset{(1)}{=}a\land 0=0.$$

Also, using (2) and $IF3)$ we have that $(a\Rightarrow c)\lor(a\land d)\in F$, so the pair $(a\Rightarrow c,a\land d)$ is in $N(H,F)$ and we can use it to define $(a,b)\to(c,d)=(a\Rightarrow c,a\land d)$.
head: environment

label: NHFessiminelsonalgebra
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{NHFessiminelsonalgebra}
If $\mathbf{H}\in\mbox{$\cal SH$}$ and $F$ is an $i$-filter of $\mathbf H$, then the system \linebreak $\langle N(H,F);$ $\sqcap,\sqcup,\to,\sim,\top \rangle$  with the operations defined as in  (V1)-(V5) is a semi-Nelson algebra.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Using that $F$ is a filter we can prove that the operations $\sqcap$, $\sqcup$, $\top$ and $\sim$ are well defined in $N(H,F)$ (see \cite{monteiro19construction}). Also, by observation \ref{buenadefdeimplicavakarelov}, it follows that the operation $\to$ is well defined. Furthermore, following the proof of Theorem 4.1 in\cite{cornejo16semiNelson},  $\mathbf{N(H,F)}$ verifies the axioms $SN1)$-$SN11)$ so it is is a semi-Nelson algebra.
head: environment

title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{16012020}
Let $\mathbf{H}\in\mbox{$\cal SH$}$. If $\mathbf S$ is a subalgebra of $\mathbf{V_k}(\mathbf{H})$, such that $\pi_1(S)=H$ (with $\pi_1$ the projection over the first component of ${V_k}(H)$), then there exists an $i$-filter $E$ of $\mathbf H$ such that $S=N(H,E)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E=\{x\in H : x=a\lor b \text{ for some } (a,b)\in S\}$. We are going to prove that $E$ is an $i$-filter.

It was shown in \cite{viglizzo99algebras} that if $\mathbf H\in\mbox{$\cal H$}$, then $E$ is a filter of $\mathbf H$. But that proof can be extended naturally to the variety $\mbox{$\cal SH$}$, because it only uses lattice properties.

Consider a dense element $x\in H$. Since $\pi_1(S)=H$, then there exists $y\in H$ such that $(x,y)\in S$. Besides, since $S$ is a subalgebra of $\mathbf{V_k(H)}$, $(0,1)\in S$, and therefore $(x,y)\to(0,1)=(x\Rightarrow0,x\land1)=(x^*,x)=(0,x)\in S$. Hence, $x\in E$ because $x=x\lor0$, and we conclude that $E$ satisfies $IF2$).

Suppose now that for $z,t\in H$ we have $z\lor t\in E$,

Since $z\lor t\in E$, there exists a pair $(a,b)\in S$ such that $z\lor t=a\lor b$. But $S$ is a subalgebra of $\mathbf{V_k(H)}$, so $\sim(a,b)=(b,a)\in S$, and therefore $(a,b)\cup(b,a)=(a\lor b,a\land b)=(a\lor b,0)\in S$. This means that $(z\lor t,0)\in S$, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{19022020_1}
    \sim(z\lor t,0)=(0,z\lor t)\in S.
\end{equation}

Using the hypothesis $\pi_1(S)=H$, and $x,z,t\in H$, it follows that there exist some $x',z',t'\in H$ such that $(x,x'), (z,z'), (t,t')\in S$. This implies that the next term belongs to $S$:
$$((x,x')\to(z,z'))\cup((x,x')\cap(t,t'))=(x\Rightarrow z,x\land z')\cup(x\land t,x'\lor t')=$$ 
\begin{equation}\label{19022020_2}
    ((x\Rightarrow z)\lor(x\land t),(x\land z')\land(x'\lor t')).
\end{equation}

Since $(x\land z')\land(x'\lor t')=(x\land z'\land x')\lor(x\land z'\land t')=0\lor(x\land z'\land t')=x\land z'\land t'$, (\ref{19022020_2}) yields
\begin{equation}\label{19022020_3}
    ((x\Rightarrow z)\lor(x\land t),x\land z'\land t')\in S.
\end{equation}

Combining (\ref{19022020_1}) with (\ref{19022020_3}) we get
\begin{equation}\label{19022020_4}
    ((x\Rightarrow z)\lor(x\land t),x\land z'\land t')\cup(0,z\lor t)=((x\Rightarrow z)\lor(x\land t),x\land z'\land t'\land(z\lor t))\in S.
\end{equation}

Since $x\land z'\land t'\land(z\lor t)=(x\land z'\land t'\land z)\land(x\land z'\land t'\land t)=(x\land t'\land(z\land z'))\lor(x\land z\land(t\land t'))=0\lor0=0$, from (\ref{19022020_4}) it follows that
$$((x\Rightarrow z)\lor(x\land t),0)\in S.$$ 

By the definition of $E$ it follows that $$(x\Rightarrow z)\lor(x\land t)\lor0=(x\Rightarrow z)\lor(x\land t)\in E.$$

Hence, $E$ is an $i$-filter.

Let us prove now that $N(H,E)=S$. It is clear that $S\subseteq N(H,E)$. If we have $(a,b)\in N(H,E)$, then $a\land b=0$, and $a\lor b\in E$, so there exists $(c,d)\in S$ such that $c\lor d=a\lor b$. Then, as before $(c,d)\cup(d,c)=(c\lor d,0)=(a\lor b,0)\in S$. On the other hand, since $\pi_1(S)=H$, there exists some $b'\in H$ such that $(b,b')\in S$, and therefore $(b,b')\to(0,1)=(b^*,b)\in S$. 
By properties of the pseudocomplement, $a\land b=0$ implies that $a\leq b^*$ and hence $(a\lor b)\land b^*=(a\land b^*)\lor(b\land b^*)=a\lor 0=a$, so we can conclude that $(a\lor b,0)\cap(b^*,b)=((a\lor b)\land b^*,0\lor b)=(a,b)\in S$.
head: environment

title: \bf Theorem
body_md: Every semi-Nelson algebra $\mathbf{A}$ is isomorphic to an algebra of the form $\mathbf{N(H,F)}$, for some semi-Heyting algebra $\mathbf{H}$ and some $i$-filter $F$ of $\mathbf{H}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Theorem \ref{isosemiHeytingsemiNelson}, every semi-Nelson algebra $\mathbf{A}$ can be obtained as a subalgebra of $\mathbf{V_k}(\mathbf{sH}(A))$, and clearly $\pi_1(\mathbf{V_k}(\mathbf{sH}(A)))=\mathbf{sH}(A)$, so $\mathbf{A}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf N(\mathbf{sH}(\mathbf A),\mathbf E)$, where $E$ is the $i$-filter of Lemma \ref{16012020}.
head: environment

label: ifiltersthatcontaindenseelem
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{ifiltersthatcontaindenseelem}
If $\mathbf{H}\in\mbox{$\cal SH$}$, and $F$ is an $i$-filter of $\mathbf H$, then $\pi_1(N(H,F))=H$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If $x\in H$, by Lemma \ref{caractdensos}, we have that $x\lor x^*\in\mathcal{D}_s(H)\subseteq F$. Also, $x\land x^*=0$ is valid, so $(x,x^*)\in N(H,F)$ and $x\in\pi_1(N(H,F))$.
head: environment

label: functorfromSHFtoSN
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{functorfromSHFtoSN}
The application $\alpha:\mathbf{sHF}\longrightarrow\mathbf{sN}$ defined on the objects of $\mathbf{sHF}$ by $\alpha((\mathbf H,F))=\mathbf{N(H,F)}$, and on morphisms by $\alpha(f)(a,b)=(f(a),f(b))$ for all $(a,b)\in N(H,F)$, is a functor from $\mathbf{sHF}$ to $\mathbf{sN}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us check that $\alpha$ is well defined. If $(\mathbf H,F)$ is an object of $\mathbf{sHF}$, then $\alpha((\mathbf H,F))=\mathbf{N(H,F)}$ is a semi-Nelson algebra due to Lemma \ref{NHFessiminelsonalgebra}.

Now we take a morphism $f:(\mathbf H,F)\longrightarrow(\mathbf H',F')$. Since $f$ is a Heyting homomorphism, we have by straightforward calculations that:
$\alpha(f)((a,b)\to(c,d))=(f(a\Rightarrow c),f(a\land d))=(f(a),f(b))\to((f(c),f(d)))=$
$\alpha(f)(a,b)\to\alpha(f)(c,d)$, and similarly for the rest of the operations. 

For all $(a,b)$ $\in$ $N(H,F)$,  $(a,b)=(Id_{(H,F)}(a),Id_{(H,F)}(b)))$, therefore $\alpha(Id_{(\mathbf H,F)})=Id_{\alpha(\mathbf H,F)}$.

Finally, for any two given morphisms $f:(\mathbf H',F')\longrightarrow(\mathbf H'',F'')$, and $g:(\mathbf H,F)\longrightarrow(\mathbf H',F')$, we have that  for all $(a,b)\in N(H,F)$, $\alpha(f\circ g)(a,b)=((f\circ g)(a),(f\circ g)(b))=(f(g(a)),f(g(b)))=\alpha(f)((g(a),g(b)))=((\alpha(f))\circ(\alpha(g)))(a,b)$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Let $A\in\mbox{$\cal SN$}$. We say that an element $a\in A$ is \emph{positive} if $ \sim a\leq a$. We denote by $A^+$ the set of positive elements of $A$.
head: environment

label: formadelospositivos
title: \bf Observation
body_md:
\label{formadelospositivos}
If $A\in\mbox{$\cal SN$}$, then $A^+=\{x\lor\sim x : x\in A\}$. Indeed, if $x\in A^+$, then $\sim x\leq x$, so $x=x\lor\sim x$. On the other hand, if $y=x\lor\sim x$, by $SN$\ref{identidad_ditrib_neg}) and $SN$\ref{identidad_kleene}) it follows that $y=x\lor\sim x\geq x\land\sim x=\sim(\sim x\lor x)=\sim y$.
head: environment

label: lospositivossonifiltros
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{lospositivossonifiltros}
If $\mathbf{A}\in\mbox{$\cal SN$}$, then $[\![A^+]\!]$ is an $i$-filter of $\mathbf{sH}(A)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem \ref{isosemiHeytingsemiNelson}, there exists a subalgebra $\mathbf S$ of $\mathbf{V_k}(\mathbf{sH}(A))$ such that $\mathbf A$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf S$, and the isomorphism is given by $h(a)=([\![a]\!],[\![\sim a]\!])$ for all $a\in A$. Therefore $S=\{([\![a]\!],[\![\sim a]\!]) : a\in A\}$. Then, it is immediate that $\pi_1(S)=\mathbf{sH}(A)$.

By Lemma \ref{16012020}, $S=N(\mathbf{sH}(A),E)$, where $E=\{[\![a]\!]\lor[\![\sim a]\!] : a\in A\}$ is an $i$-filter of $\mathbf{sH}(\mathbf A)$. But $E=[\![A^+]\!]$, due to observation \ref{formadelospositivos}, which completes the proof.
head: environment

label: functorfromSNtoSHF
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{functorfromSNtoSHF}
The application $\beta:\mathbf{sN}\longrightarrow\mathbf{sHF}$ defined on the objects of $\mathbf{sN}$ by $\beta(\mathbf{A})=(\mathbf{sH}(\mathbf A),[\![A^+]\!])$, and on morphisms  $f:A\longrightarrow A'$ by $\beta(f)([\![a]\!])=[\![f(a)]\!]$ for all $a\in A$,  is a  functor from $\mathbf{sN}$ to $\mathbf{sHF}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us check that $\beta$ is well defined. For an object $\mathbf{A}$ of $\mathbf{sN}$, $\mathbf{sH}(\mathbf{A})$ is a semi-Heyting algebra, and by Lemma \ref{lospositivossonifiltros} we have that $[\![A^+]\!]$ is an $i$-filter of $\mathbf{sH}(\mathbf{A})$.
Therefore, $(\mathbf{sH}(A),[\![A^+]\!])$ is an object in $\mathbf{sHF}$.

For any semi-Nelson morphism $f:A\longrightarrow A'$, we calculate:
$ \beta(f)([\![a\to b]\!])=$
$[\![f(a\to b)]\!]=$ $[\![f(a)\to f(b)]\!]=$ $[\![f(a)]\!]\Rightarrow[\![f(b)]\!]=$ 
$\beta(f)([\![a]\!])\Rightarrow\beta(f)([\![b]\!])$,
 and similarly for the other operations.

Also, if $[\![x]\!]\in [\![A^+]\!]$, then by observation \ref{formadelospositivos} we can write $[\![x]\!]=$ $[\![y\lor$ $\sim y]\!]$, for some $y\in A$, and so $\beta(f)([\![x]\!])=\beta(f)([\![y\lor\sim y]\!])=\beta(f)([\![y]\!])\cup\beta(f)([\![\sim y]\!])=[\![f(y)]\!]\cup[\![f(\sim y)]\!]=$ $[\![f(y)]\!]\cup[\![\sim f(y)]\!]=$ $[\![f(y)\lor\sim f(y)]\!]$. Since $f(y)\in f(A)\subseteq A'$, it follows that $\beta(f)([\![x]\!])\in [\![A'^+]\!]$. This shows that $\beta(f)([\![A^+]\!])\subseteq [\![A'^+]\!]$, so $\beta(f)$ is a morphism in $\mathbf{sHF}$.

It is straightforward to check that $\beta$ preserves identities and compositions, so it is indeed a functor.
head: environment

title: \bf Theorem
body_md: The functors $\alpha$ and $\beta$ establish an equivalence between the categories $\mathbf{sHF}$ and $\mathbf{sN}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Notice that $\beta\alpha(\mathbf{A},F)=\beta(\mathbf{N(\mathbf{A},F)})=(\mathbf{sH(N(\mathbf{A},F))},[\![N(A,F)^+]\!])$, with $\mathbf{sH(N(\mathbf{A},F))} =\{[\![(x,y)]\!] : (x,y)\in N(A,F)\}=
\{[\![(x,y)]\!] : x,y\in A, x\land y=0, x\lor y\in F \}$.

We define now $\eta_A(x)=[\![(x,x^*)]\!]$, for each object $\mathbf{A}$ of $\mathbf{sHF}$ and for all $x\in A$, and we prove that $\eta=\{\eta_A\}$ is a natural isomorphism from $id_\mathbf{sHF}$ to $\beta\alpha$.

$\eta_A$ is well defined: Since $x\land x^*=0$ and also $\mathcal{D}_s(A)\subseteq F$ it follows that $x\lor x^*\in \mathcal{D}_s(A)\subseteq F$. Hence, $(x,x^*)\in N(A,F)$.

$\eta_A$ is surjective:    
    If $[\![(x,y)]\!]\in\beta\alpha(A,F)$, then $[\![(x,y)]\!]=[\![(x,x^*)]\!]$. Indeed, since $(x,y)\to(x,x^*)=(x\Rightarrow x,$ $x\land x^*)=(1,0)$ and $(x,x^*)\to(x,y)=(x\Rightarrow x,x\land y)=(1,0)$, so by definition we have that $[\![(x,y)]\!]=[\![(x,x^*)]\!]$. Therefore $\eta_A(x)=[\![(x,y)]\!]$.
    
   $\eta_A$ is injective:
        If $[\![(x,x^*)]\!]=[\![(y,y^*)]\!]$, then $(x,x^*)\to(y,y^*)=(x\Rightarrow y,x\land y^*)=(1,0)$. Therefore, from $x\Rightarrow y=1$, using properties of semi-Heyting algebras we obtain $x\leq y$. Analogously, $(y,y^*)\to(x,x^*)=$ $(y\Rightarrow x,y\land x^*)=(1,0)$ implies $y\leq x$.
        
    $\eta_A$ is a $\mathbf{sHF}$-morphism:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\eta_A(x)\cup\eta_A(y)=[\![(x,x^*)]\!]\cup[\![(y,y^*)]\!]=[\![(x,x^*)\sqcup(y,y^*)]\!]=[\![(x\lor y,x^*\land y^*)]\!]=[\![(x\lor y,$ $(x\lor y)^*)]\!]=\eta_A(x\lor y)$.
        \item $\eta_A(x)\cap\eta_A(y)=[\![(x,x^*)]\!]\cap[\![(y,y^*)]\!]=[\![(x,x^*)\sqcap(y,y^*)]\!]=[\![(x\land y,x^*\lor y^*)]\!]$. Also, $\eta_A(x\land y)=[\![(x\land y,(x\land y)^*)]\!]$. Since $(x\land y,x^*\lor y^*)\to(x\land y,(x\land y)^*)=((x\land y)\Rightarrow(x\land y),(x\land y)\land(x\land y)^*)=(1,0)$ and $(x\land y,(x\land y)^*)\to(x\land y,x^*\lor y^*)=((x\land y)\Rightarrow(x\land y),(x\land y)\land(x^*\lor y^*))=(1,(x\land y\land x^*)\lor(x\land y \land y^*))=(1,0)$, we have that $\eta_A(x)\cap\eta_A(y)=\eta_A(x\land y)$.
        \item $\eta_A(x)\Rightarrow \eta_A(y)=[\![(x,x^*)]\!]\Rightarrow[\![(y,y^*)]\!]=[\![(x,x^*)\Rightarrow(y,y^*)]\!]=[\![(x\Rightarrow y,x\land y^*)]\!]$. Also, $\eta_A(x\Rightarrow y)=[\![(x\Rightarrow y,(x\Rightarrow y)^*)]\!]$. Since $(x\Rightarrow y,x\land y^*)\to(x\Rightarrow y,(x\Rightarrow y)^*)=((x\Rightarrow y)\Rightarrow(x\Rightarrow y),(x\Rightarrow y)\land(x\Rightarrow y)^*)=(1,0)$ and $(x\Rightarrow y,(x\Rightarrow y)^*)\to(x\Rightarrow y,x\land y^*)=((x\Rightarrow y)\Rightarrow(x\Rightarrow y),(x\Rightarrow y)\land (x\land y^*))\underset{SH\ref{infimoeimplicaSH})}{=}(1,x\land (y\land y^*))=(1,0)$, we have that $[\![(x\Rightarrow y,x\land y^*)]\!]=[\![(x\Rightarrow y,(x\Rightarrow y)^*)]\!]$. Therefore, we conclude that $\eta_A(x)\Rightarrow \eta_A(y)=\eta_A(x\Rightarrow y)$.
        \item $\eta_A(F)\subseteq [\![N(A,F)^+]\!]$
            
        If $y\in\eta_A(F)$, then $y=\eta_A(x)$, for some $x\in F$. Hence, $y=[\![(x,x^*)]\!]$, with $x\in F$.
        
        We observe that for $x\in F$, we have that $(x,0)\in N(A,F)$. Besides, $[\![(x,x^*)]\!]=[\![(x,0)]\!]$ because $(x,0)\to(x,x^*)=(x\Rightarrow x,x\land x^*)=(1,0)$ and $(x,x^*)\to(x,0)=(x\Rightarrow x,x\land 0)=(1,0)$.
            
        Therefore, we can write $y=[\![(x,0)]\!]$. Now, since $\sim(x,0)=(0,x)\leq(x,0)$, it follows that $(x,0)\in N(A,F)^+$, and hence $y\in [\![N(A,F)^+]\!]$.
    \end{itemize}
Finally, we check the naturality of $\eta$, that is, the following diagram commutes:
		\begin{displaymath}
		\xymatrix{ A \ar[rr]^{\eta_A}\ar[d]_{f} && \beta\alpha(A) \ar[d]^{\beta\alpha(f)} \\
			A' \ar[rr]^{\eta_{A'}} && \beta\alpha(A')  }
		\end{displaymath}
    
    Notice that since $\eta_A$ is an isomorphism, $\eta_A^{-1}([\![(x,y)]\!])=x$ for every $x\in A$. Then we have $$(\eta_{A'}^{-1}\circ \beta\alpha(f)\circ\eta_A)(x)=\eta_{A'}^{-1}(\beta\alpha(f)([\![(x,0)]\!]))=$$
    $$=\eta_{A'}^{-1}([\![\alpha(f)(x,0)]\!])=\eta_{A'}^{-1}([\![f(x),0)]\!]=f(x).$$
    
Thus $f=\eta_{A'}^{-1}\circ \beta\alpha(f)\circ\eta_A$, and therefore $\eta_{A'}\circ f=\beta\alpha(f)\circ\eta_A$.

Now we consider the functor $\alpha\beta$, which transforms every object $\mathbf A$ of $\mathbf{sN}$ into $\mathbf{ N(sH(A),[\![A^+]\!])}$. On a morphism $f:A\longrightarrow A'$ it is defined by  $\alpha\beta(f)([\![x]\!],[\![y]\!])=([\![f(x)]\!],[\![f(y)]\!])$. We define for each object $\mathbf A$ of $\mathbf{sN}$, $\delta_A:A\longrightarrow \mathbf{ N(sH(A),[\![A^+]\!])}$  by $\delta_A(x)=([\![x]\!],[\![\sim x]\!])$.

{$\delta_A$ is well defined:}
        On the one hand, $[\![x]\!]\cap[\![\sim x]\!]=[\![x\land\sim x]\!]=[\![0]\!]$, because $(x\land\sim x)\to 0=(x\land\sim x)\to (x\land\sim x\land0)=(x\land\sim x)\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $} 0=1$ and $0\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $} (x\land\sim x)=1$ by well known properties of Nelson algebras.
    On the other hand, using $SN$\ref{identidad_kleene}) and De Morgan properties we have $\sim(x\lor\sim x)=\sim x\land x\leq x\lor\sim x$, so $x\lor\sim x\in A^+$. Therefore $[\![x]\!]\cup[\![\sim x]\!]=[\![x\lor\sim x]\!]\in [\![A^+]\!]$.

    {$\delta_A$ is surjective:}
        If $([\![x]\!],[\![y]\!])\in\alpha\beta(A,F)$, then $([\![x]\!],[\![y]\!])=([\![x]\!],[\![\sim x]\!])$. Indeed, this is a consequence of $([\![x]\!],[\![y]\!])\to([\![x]\!],[\![\sim x]\!])=([\![x]\!]\Rightarrow [\![x]\!],[\![x]\!]\cap [\![\sim x]\!])=([\![1]\!],[\![x\land\sim x]\!])=([\![1]\!],[\![0]\!])$ and $([\![x]\!],[\![\sim x]\!])\to([\![x]\!],[\![y]\!])=([\![x]\!]\Rightarrow [\![x]\!],[\![x]\!]\cap [\![y]\!])=([\![1]\!],[\![0]\!])$. Therefore $\delta_A(x)=([\![x]\!],[\![y]\!])$.
    
    {$\delta_A$ is injective:}
        If $([\![x]\!],[\![\sim x]\!])=([\![y]\!],[\![\sim y]\!])$, then $[\![x]\!]=[\![y]\!]$ and $[\![\sim x]\!]=[\![\sim y]\!]$, so we have the following: $x\to y=1$, $y\to x=1$, $\sim x\to \sim y=1$, $\sim y\to \sim x=1$. By proposition \ref{propertiesseminelson} (\ref{equivalenciadeclasesnelson}), we have that $x\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $} y=1$, $y\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $} x=1$, $\sim x\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $} \sim y=1$, $\sim y\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $} \sim x=1$, which implies (see for example \cite{viglizzo99algebras}, (1.15)) that $x=y$.
    
    {$\delta_A$ is a $\mathbf{sN}$-morphism:}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\delta_A(x)\sqcup\delta_A(y)=([\![x]\!],[\![\sim x]\!])\sqcup([\![y]\!],[\![\sim y]\!])=([\![x]\!]\cup[\![y]\!],[\![\sim x]\!]\cap[\![\sim y]\!])=([\![x\lor y]\!],[\![\sim x\land\sim y]\!])=([\![x\lor y]\!],[\![\sim (x\lor y)]\!])=\delta_A(x\lor y)$. In a similar manner we can prove that $\delta_A(x)\sqcap\delta_A(y)=\delta_A(x\land y)$.
        \item $\sim\delta_A(x)=\sim([\![x]\!],[\![\sim x]\!])=([\![\sim x]\!],[\![x]\!])=\delta_A(\sim x)$.
        \item $\delta_A(x)\to \delta_A(y)=([\![x]\!],[\![\sim x]\!])\to([\![y]\!],[\![\sim y]\!])=([\![x]\!]\Rightarrow[\![y]\!],[\![x]\!]\cap[\![\sim y]\!])=([\![x\to y]\!],[\![x\land\sim y]\!])$.
        
        By $SN$\ref{identidad_semi_neg_implica_impl}) and $SN$\ref{identidad_semi_impl_implica_neg}), we see that $[\![x\land\sim y]\!]=[\![\sim(x\to y)]\!]$. Hence $\delta_A(x)\to \delta_A(y)=([\![x\to y]\!],[\![x\land\sim y]\!])=([\![x\to y]\!],[\![\sim(x\to y)]\!])=\delta_A(x\to y)$.
    \end{itemize}
    
    Finally, $\delta$ is a natural transformation: to see that this diagram commutes, 
    	\begin{displaymath}
    	\xymatrix{ A \ar[rr]^{\delta_A}\ar[d]_{f} && \alpha\beta(A) \ar[d]^{\alpha\beta(f)} \\
    		A' \ar[rr]^{\delta_{A'}} && \alpha\beta(A')  }
    	\end{displaymath}
    we calculate
        $\alpha\beta(f)\circ\delta_A(x)=\alpha\beta(f)([\![x]\!],[\![\sim x]\!])=([\![f(x)]\!],[\![f(\sim x)]\!])=([\![f(x)]\!],[\![\sim f(x)]\!])=\delta_{A'}\circ f(x)$.

title: \bf Lemma
body_md: Let $\mathbf{A}\in\mbox{$\cal DSN$}$. If we consider the equivalence relation $\equiv$ defined in section \ref{quotients}, then that relation is compatible with respect of the operation $'$. Hence, $\equiv$ is a congruence in $\mbox{$\cal DSN$}$.

label: def_op_vak_tic
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def_op_vak_tic}
Let $\mathbf{A}=\langle A;\cap,\cup,\Rightarrow,^\dagger,\bot,\top \rangle\in\mbox{$\cal DSH$}$. For $(a,b)\in V_k(A)$ we define the following unary operation on $V_k(A)$: $$(a,b)'=(a^\dagger,b\cap(a^\dagger\Rightarrow a)).$$
head: environment

title: \bf Theorem
body_md: If $\mathbf{A}\in\mbox{$\cal DSH$}$, then the system $\mathbf{V_k(A)}=\langle V_k(A); \sqcap,\sqcup,\to,\sim,',\top\rangle$ is a dually hemimorphic semi-Nelson algebra.
head: environment

label: isoduallysemiHeytingsemiNelson
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{isoduallysemiHeytingsemiNelson} {\rm \cite{cornejo19dually} }
If $\mathbf{A}\in\mbox{$\cal DSH$}$, then $\mathbf{A}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf{dsH}(\mathbf{V_k}(\mathbf A))$. Also, if $\mathbf{A}\in\mbox{$\cal DSN$}$, then $\mathbf{A}$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of $\mathbf{V_k(dsH(A))}$.
head: environment

label: duallyheminelsonarecentered
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{duallyheminelsonarecentered}
If $\mathbf A\in\mbox{$\cal DSN$}$, then $\mathbf A$ is centered, with center $1'$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We want to prove that $\sim 1'=1'$, or equivalently, the following conditions holds simultaneously:
\[
    \sim 1'\to1'=1,\
    1'\to\sim1'=1,
\]
\begin{equation}\label{19922020_5}
    \sim1'\to\sim(\sim1')=1,\
    \sim(\sim1')\to\sim1'=1.
\end{equation}

By Proposition \ref{propertiesseminelson} (\ref{equivalenciadeclasesnelson}), (\ref{19922020_5}) is equivalent to
\[
    \sim 1'\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}1'=1,\
    1'\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}\sim1'=1,\
\]
\[
    \sim1'\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}\sim(\sim1')=1,\
    \sim(\sim1')\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}\sim1'=1,
\]
which is equivalent to show that
\begin{equation}\label{19922020_6}
    \sim 1'\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}1'=1,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{19922020_7}
    1'\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}\sim1'=1.
\end{equation}

By \textit{(DSN\ref{dhsn_4})}, \textit{(DSN\ref{dhsn_5})}, and proposition \ref{equivalenciadeclasesnelson}, we have that $\sim 1'\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}(\sim 1\land(1'\to 1))=1$, that is (1) $\sim 1'\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}0=1$. Since in every Nelson algebra $0\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $} x=x$ holds for all $x$, it follows that (2) $0\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $} 1'=1'$. By (1), (2) and proposition \ref{propertiesseminelson} (\ref{transitivitynelson}), we have that $\sim 1'\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}1'=1$, which proves \eqref{19922020_6}.

By \textit{(DSN\ref{dhsn_2})} we have (3) $1=1'\to \sim1=1'\to0=1'\to(1'\land0)=1'\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}0$. Using again that $0\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $} 1'=1'$, and proposition \ref{propertiesseminelson} (\ref{transitivitynelson}), gives us $\sim 1'\mbox{$\ \to_\text {\tiny N}\ $}1=1$, which proves \eqref{19922020_7}.
head: environment

label: isoduallysemiNelson
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{isoduallysemiNelson}
If $\mathbf{A}\in\mbox{$\cal DSN$}$, then $\mathbf{A}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf{V_k(dsH(A))}$.
head: environment

title: \bf Observation
body_md:
Another way of proving Theorem \ref{isoduallysemiNelson} is the following: if we consider the structure $\mathbf{N(H,E)}$ as in Lemma \ref{16012020}, and take $\mathbf{H}\in\mbox{$\cal DSH$}$, we have no guarantee that this set is going to be a closed under the operation $^\dagger$. If instead we consider a subalgebra $\mathbf S$ such that $\pi_1(S)=H$, then the proof indicated in the lemma still holds for the variety $\mbox{$\cal DSH$}$, since it does not use the operations $'$ or $^\dagger$. Hence, the sets $S$ and $N(H,E)$ are equal, so $N(H,E)$ inherits the operations from $\mathbf S$. Indeed, due to Theorem \ref{isoduallysemiHeytingsemiNelson}, we know that the function $h:A\to \mathbf{V_k}(\mathbf{dsH}(A))$ defined by $h(a)=([\![a]\!],[\![\sim a]\!])$ is a monomorphism. Hence, $A\cong h(A)$. Let us take then the subalgebra $\mathbf S=h(\mathbf A)$ of $\mathbf{V_k}(\mathbf{dsH}(\mathbf A))$. It is immediate that $\pi_1(S)=\mathbf{dsH}(A)$. Therefore, by Lemma \ref{16012020}, $h(\mathbf  A)=\mathbf{N(dsH(A),E)}$ for $E=\{[\![x]\!]\in \mathbf{dsH}(A):[\![x]\!]=[\![a]\!]\lor [\![b]\!],([\![a]\!],[\![b]\!])\in S\}$.

Since $\mathbf S$ is a subalgebra of $\mathbf{V_k}(\mathbf{dsH}(\mathbf A))$, we have that $([\![1]\!],[\![0]\!])\in S$, so the center $([\![0]\!],[\![0]\!])=([\![1]\!],[\![0]\!])'$ is an element of $S$. Then $[\![0]\!]=[\![0]\!]\lor[\![0]\!]\in E$. Since $E$ is a filter, this shows that $E=\mathbf{dsH}(A)$.

We have proved that $S=N(\mathbf{dsH}(A),\mathbf{dsH}(A))=\mathbf{V_k}(\mathbf{dsH}(A))$, and therefore $h$ is an isomorphism.
